assessment.nobel_worthiness: Circuit QED made strong, controllable light-matter coupling available on a chip: a superconducting artificial atom coupled to a single microwave resonator mode, enabling dispersive readout, photon-number resolution, and the architecture of essentially all superconducting quantum processors. It opened a genuinely new regime (strong coupling with engineered atoms) and has been reproduced and extended in many laboratories. I declare that this is my own field, so I weigh it with caution, but the discovery-level importance is clear.
assessment.attribution: The theory proposal (Blais, Huang, Wallraff, Girvin, Schoelkopf, 2004) and the first strong-coupling experiment (Wallraff et al., Nature 2004) are the decisive contributions. Schoelkopf and Wallraff led the experimental realization; Blais is the lead theorist of the proposal. Girvin is also a key theorist and would be a painful omission; with a limit of three I choose the lead theorist and the two experimental leaders. Credit among the theory authors is unresolved.
assessment.maturity: Two decades of independent confirmation across many groups and platforms; the interpretation is stable. Timing is good, particularly after the 2025 prize for macroscopic quantum tunnelling in circuits, which recognised the device physics while leaving the light-matter architecture unrecognised. Some may see it as too close to the 2025 award, while others see it as the natural complement.
uncertainties: Allocation among Blais, Girvin, Schoelkopf and Wallraff, and between theory and experiment, is contestable.
Overlap with the 2025 prize may be thought to reduce the need for further circuit-based recognition.
My own proximity to the field and to some of these people could bias my assessment.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Quantum key distribution (BB84, E91) turned the no-cloning and entanglement properties of quantum mechanics into a cryptographic principle and launched experimental quantum communication. It is conceptually clear, original, and has spawned a large experimental programme and commercial systems; it is also tied to foundations through Bell tests.
assessment.attribution: Bennett and Brassard (BB84) are the clear originators of quantum cryptography; Ekert independently proposed the entanglement-based protocol in 1991. Wiesner's earlier conjugate-coding idea complicates the history, but he is not in the credited names. The trio is the natural configuration within the supplied credit.
assessment.maturity: Protocols have been demonstrated over fibre and satellite links in many laboratories; the underlying physics is settled. Recognition is long overdue rather than premature. The question is whether the committee regards it as physics rather than information science.
uncertainties: Practical security of real devices (side channels) is a separate issue from the principle being recognised.
Wiesner's precursor and the Ekert-versus-BB84 priority are open allocation questions.
Whether the committee views this as sufficiently within physics.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The Cirac-Zoller proposal for quantum gates with trapped ions, and the broader Cirac-Zoller programme for analogue and digital quantum simulation with cold atoms, provided the blueprint for two of the leading quantum-technology platforms. The originality and lasting influence are exceptional, and the theory was directly realised experimentally.
assessment.attribution: A natural two-person configuration. The credit is clean for the 1995 gate proposal; the experimental realisation (Wineland, Blatt, and others) is outside the supplied names, and Wineland has already been recognised in 2012.
assessment.maturity: Experimental confirmation is extensive in ions, neutral atoms and Rydberg systems. The theory has been validated repeatedly, though the 2012 prize partly covers the ion-control side. Timing is reasonable, since neither has been recognised.
uncertainties: A prize may be seen as partly duplicating the 2012 prize for manipulating single quantum systems.
Overlap with the Hubbard-simulation candidate (B015) means the committee must avoid double counting.
A theory-only prize may be less compelling when the key experiments were separately rewarded.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The optical lattice clock, with atoms trapped at a magic wavelength, delivers clock stability and accuracy at the 10^-18 level, enabling tests of fundamental physics, relativistic geodesy and a redefinition of the second. It is a clear case of an enabling device grounded in precise physical detail.
assessment.attribution: Katori proposed the magic-wavelength lattice concept and demonstrated the first clocks; Ye brought the clock to extreme accuracy and spectroscopic coherence. Ye also appears under other candidates, which does not change the clock credit. Hall and Hänsch (2005) and Wineland (2012) were already recognised for adjacent work, and Ludlow, Ye, and others are not on this list.
assessment.maturity: Independent comparison between laboratories in several countries confirms performance; the redefinition of the second is still pending, which suggests the application is ahead of the discovery. The science is mature.
uncertainties: Whether the committee sees this as a refinement of the already-recognised precision measurement prizes.
Other contributors to the clock development are not in the credited names.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Ground-state cooling and quantum control of mechanical oscillators extends quantum mechanics to massive objects: sideband cooling, entanglement of mechanical modes, and quantum state transfer. It pushes the question of how far quantum behaviour extends and connects to superconducting qubits and sensors, which is close to my own interests.
assessment.attribution: Cleland demonstrated quantum control of a mechanical resonator coupled to a superconducting qubit, while Aspelmeyer and Kippenberg developed cavity optomechanics. The three names are plausible, but important contributors such as Painter, Lehnert, Schwab, and Harris are not in the credited set, so credit is fragmented.
assessment.maturity: Ground-state cooling and entanglement have been reproduced in several platforms and the basic physics is well established. Some of the most interesting results, such as macroscopic entanglement and gravity tests, are still developing.
uncertainties: The field has many co-equal contributors, making a three-person allocation difficult.
Distinguishing the discovery from technique development is not straightforward.
Parts of the implications, such as tests of quantum gravity, are not yet realised.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The magic-angle theory and the discovery of correlated insulators and superconductivity in twisted bilayer graphene opened an entirely new field of tunable correlated electron physics (moire materials). It is original and has a large footprint. I defer to colleagues with condensed-matter expertise on details.
assessment.attribution: Bistritzer and MacDonald predicted the flat band at the magic angle; Jarillo-Herrero's group made the experimental discovery. The credited trio matches the theory-plus-experiment pairing, though Cao, Fatemi and others who did the experiment, and the earlier work of Lopes dos Santos, Peres and Castro Neto, are relevant to attribution.
assessment.maturity: Strong independent replication, with the field growing rapidly. The interpretation of the superconductivity is not yet settled, and the field is evolving quickly, so some might feel it is slightly early.
uncertainties: The pairing mechanism in the superconducting phase is unresolved.
Credit for the theory (Lopes dos Santos et al.) and for the experimental team is disputed.
Possibly premature relative to older candidates.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Rydberg blockade underpins programmable neutral-atom arrays that now serve as quantum simulators and processors, with high-fidelity gates and demonstrations of exotic many-body states. The step from a blockade proposal to controllable arrays is a clear passage from basic physics to platform.
assessment.attribution: The blockade proposal (Jaksch et al., Lukin et al.) and the first demonstrations (Grangier, Browaeys, Saffman) are spread across many people. I include Browaeys, Grangier and Lukin as the strongest experimental-and-proposal combination within the supplied names, but Saffman and others are plausible, and the list shows four names so one must be left out.
assessment.maturity: Rapid progress and replication across groups, but the field is still maturing; error correction and scaling remain open and the most important results are recent. Probably early.
uncertainties: Four credited names must be reduced to three, and the exclusion of Saffman is contestable.
Many other contributors, such as Jaksch, Zoller, Weiss and Bernien, are not credited.
Maturity is still low compared with other candidates.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The proposal and realisation of spin qubits in quantum dots (Loss-DiVincenzo 1998; control by Vandersypen and others) established a scalable platform compatible with semiconductor technology, and the DiVincenzo criteria shaped the whole quantum-computing field.
assessment.attribution: Loss and DiVincenzo supplied the proposal, and Vandersypen led key experimental demonstrations. Experimental pioneers such as Kouwenhoven and Marcus, and Petta, are not in the credited names, so the experimental credit is only partly captured.
assessment.maturity: Silicon and germanium spin qubits now reach high fidelity and have been reproduced widely, but the platform is still competing with others and the long-term role is uncertain. The proposal is mature, though the application is still unresolved.
uncertainties: Experimental credit is shared with several groups not included in the credited names.
The platform's eventual significance relative to superconducting and ion-based systems is unknown.
The field's contributions might be better recognised through broader quantum-information-oriented prizes.
